clue.text: Calais menu misprinted part of sentence

indicators.note: a misprint jumbles the type, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: the ten letters of the two words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A tourist in a French port frowns at a badly printed restaurant menu.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the principal clause of a sentence is the one that can stand alone, a key component of it.

clue.text: Revealed appropriate costume

parts.note: a secret that is out has been revealed
fit means suitable or proper

explanation.surface: Someone unveils a costume that suits the occasion perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: An outfit is a set of clothes worn together, which is what a costume is.

clue.text: Eileen, going on vacation, ordered dressing-gown

indicators.note: ordered here means arranged afresh, putting the letters into a new sequence

parts.note: the name taken as written

indicators.note: a place on vacation is emptied, so the word loses everything between its outer letters

parts.note: only the first and last letters of the word survive once it is emptied

explanation.surface: A woman called Eileen, about to go on holiday, buys herself a dressing-gown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going on vacation' reads as Eileen leaving for a holiday; really 'going' is the word being emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: A negligee is a light, flimsy robe worn by women over nightclothes, a kind of dressing-gown.

clue.text: Relatively thick, studies Educating Rita at first

parts.note: a den is a private room for work, a study

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of each of the words just before it

parts.note: the initial letters of the two words of the play's title

explanation.surface: A critic judges that someone poring over the play Educating Rita finds it rather heavy going.
explanation.walkthrough: Educating Rita is a Willy Russell play and film about a hairdresser studying literature.
explanation.definitionFit: Denser is the comparative form of dense, meaning thicker or more compact than something else.

clue.text: Barber so excited for sponge?

indicators.note: excited suggests agitation, stirring things into a different arrangement

parts.note: the letters of both words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A barber is so thrilled about something, perhaps a new sponge for the salon.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge soaks up liquid, so it is a thing that takes in water by soaking.

clue.text: Why, reportedly, nobleman almost gets 12 months

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter
reportedly means as it is said, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: the letter Y is pronounced like the word why
an earl is a British nobleman

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a nobleman only nearly reaches a twelve-month milestone.
explanation.definitionFit: A calendar unit consists of twelve months, the time Earth takes to orbit the Sun.

clue.text: Age certain band from the Eighties

parts.note: an era is an age or period
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A confident claim about which decade a pop group belongs to.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasure is the British synth-pop duo of Vince Clarke and Andy Bell, whose hits began in the mid-1980s.

clue.text: Fashion magazine's article covering your setter's town in Cheshire

indicators.note: in a down clue covering means sitting on top, so the setter's piece comes before the article

parts.note: Elle is a fashion magazine, and the possessive adds the S
the setter refers to themself as me
a report is a newspaper article

explanation.surface: A style magazine runs a piece about the setter's home town in Cheshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheshire is a county in north-west England; Ellesmere Port is an industrial town there on the Manchester Ship Canal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellesmere Port is a real place in that northwestern English county, located on the Wirral peninsula.

clue.text: Assemble without idiot from Wales ultimately making signs

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a word is taken away from the first word

parts.note: taken as written
an ass is a fool

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, pointing to the last letter of each of the two words before it

parts.note: the final letters of from and Wales

explanation.surface: Someone puts together signage without help from a foolish Welshman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From Wales' looks like it describes the idiot, but both words simply give their last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Emblems are symbols or badges standing for something, so they are signs in that sense.

clue.text: I shan't eclipse renovated holy site

indicators.note: renovating a building rebuilds it, so the letters are put back together differently

parts.note: all thirteen letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone vows not to outshine a restored sacred building.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'renovated' describe the holy site, which fits the famous restoration of its frescoes.
explanation.definitionFit: The papal chapel in the Vatican, painted by Michelangelo, is a consecrated place of worship.

clue.text: Tips left with plugs

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
and means together with
to plug a hole is to fill it

explanation.surface: Advice about plugs left over, as if from a handyman.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a tip is a rubbish dump, not advice or a gratuity.
explanation.definitionFit: A landfill is a site where waste is buried, which British speakers call a rubbish tip.

clue.text: To an extent, Balrog respects other monsters

indicators.note: to an extent means partly, so only a stretch of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: Tolkien's fiery demon, the Balrog, grudgingly respects some of its fellow monsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Other' is fair because a Balrog is itself a monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogres are man-eating giants of folklore, creatures as monstrous as the Balrog itself.

clue.text: Croatian city break

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a port on the Dalmatian coast
second meaning: to crack or divide

explanation.surface: A holiday advert for a short trip to a city in Croatia.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an Adriatic port and is also a verb meaning to crack or divide into parts.

clue.text: Dress hiding one supermarket biscuit

indicators.note: something hiding an item keeps it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: garb is clothing
the Roman numeral for one
Aldi is a discount supermarket chain

explanation.surface: A shopper conceals a packet of biscuits in their dress at the supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: A garibaldi is a British biscuit of currants pressed between thin layers of dough.
explanation.definitionFit: This flat currant-filled biscuit, named after the Italian general, is a staple of British tea tins.

clue.text: Scientific establishment's work in the US supported by a politician

indicators.note: in a down clue being supported by means resting on top, so the later pieces go underneath

parts.note: the American spelling of labour
taken as written
a Tory is a British Conservative politician

explanation.surface: An American research institute is bankrolled by a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A lab is a room or building equipped for experiments and research, a place where science is done.

clue.text: Ape, bird, and others from the East

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless Australian bird

indicators.note: coming from the east in an across answer means travelling right to left, the opposite way

parts.note: et al is the Latin abbreviation for and others

explanation.surface: A list of animals: an ape, a bird and other creatures from the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ape' poses as one animal in a list, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to copy or mimic them, which is what imitating them means.

clue.text: Perhaps Mr Hyde faltered, ignoring outsiders on leave

indicators.note: ignoring the outsiders means dropping the first and last letters of the word

parts.note: taken as written
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Perhaps Mr Hyde wavered when he was about to go on leave.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's story Mr Hyde is Dr Jekyll's second self, the classic example of a person's other identity.

clue.text: Responsive to treatment, cut bad ulcer out

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged
cut means shortened, so the next word loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doctor advises that a nasty ulcer can be treated by cutting it out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like surgery; 'cut' trims a word and 'out' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A condition that can be healed by medical care is one that responds well when treated.

clue.text: Scoundrel lazily pens note in a truthful manner

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, as animals in a pen, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man
N is short for note
idly means without effort or purpose

explanation.surface: A rogue idly writes a note that turns out to be surprisingly honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking candidly means speaking frankly and openly, which is speaking honestly.

clue.text: English agreed coach is seeing problem

parts.note: E is short for English
yes is a word of agreement
to train someone is to coach them

explanation.surface: An English sports coach admits to having a problem with his vision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a person or a bus, but here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Tired, aching vision from too much reading or screen use is a visual complaint, a sight difficulty.

clue.text: Towards the back like figure stopped by king

parts.note: as means like

indicators.note: something stopped by an obstacle has it lodged within, so one letter is plugged inside

parts.note: a figure is a number, here ten
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A king halts a figure who seems to be moving backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship this nautical term means at or towards the rear, the stern.

clue.text: Group of motorists starts to rile generous hosts — oh no!

parts.note: the AA is the Automobile Association, a British motoring organisation

indicators.note: starts point to the opening letter of each of the words that follow

parts.note: the initial letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A coach party of drivers manages to annoy their kind hosts, to someone's dismay.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cry of frustration or horror, the same exclamation as a despairing groan of dismay.

clue.text: Jerboa regularly follows a second simple organism

indicators.note: follows means comes after, so the animal's letters go at the end

parts.note: taken as written
a mo is a moment, a second

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A desert rodent trails a moment behind a tiny creature.
explanation.walkthrough: A jerboa is a small hopping desert rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: This shapeless single-celled creature is the textbook example of the most basic form of life.

clue.text: Furry creature's warmer in Bow

indicators.note: Bow is in London's Cockney East End, where speakers drop the opening H sound

parts.note: hotter means more warm

explanation.surface: An animal's fur keeps it warm, as if worn like a scarf.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is a district of East London; Cockney speech famously drops initial H sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: This river-dwelling mammal of the weasel family has a dense, waterproof brown coat.

clue.text: Sultrier at heart, this person's in good condition

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only its middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of the eight
this person is means I am, contracted to I'm

explanation.surface: Someone claims to be steamier at heart and in fine shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Trim describes a body that is slim and fit, or anything that is neat and well kept.

clue.text: Balding? Point to skinhead, essentially worried

indicators.note: worried means troubled or tugged about, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so its middle letters are taken

parts.note: the two central letters of the eight

explanation.surface: Is he going bald? Point to the skinhead, who looks rather anxious about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skinhead' tempts as a shaven-headed person; only its middle letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone losing the hair on the crown of their head is described by this informal idiom.

clue.text: Set off with Pooh's friend, crossing river

indicators.note: a character crossing something straddles it, so one letter sits inside the name

parts.note: Tigger is the bouncy tiger in Winnie-the-Pooh
R is short for river

explanation.surface: Winnie-the-Pooh's pal heads off on an adventure across a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To trigger something is to start it or set it in motion, as a spark sets off an explosion.

clue.text: Defamation involving artist in favour of freedom?

indicators.note: involving means wrapping in, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: libel is written defamation
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A defamation case against an artist raises questions about free expression.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is loose: the word comes from Latin liber, free.
explanation.definitionFit: A liberal outlook supports individual rights and tolerance, valuing personal liberty.
